JSON: Name: pana_pam_phase_strain_fibers Title: Controlled antisolvent-induced microphase separation and strain-programming of PANa–PAM composite hydrogel fibers to produce spider-silk-like hierarchical architecture and improved mechanical and actuation performance Short Hypothesis: Applying antisolvent-induced microphase separation (using a methanol-rich coagulation bath) to UHMW PANa–PAM hydrogel spinning dopes and subsequently applying uniaxial post-drawing to 200–400% at elevated humidity produces hydrogen-bonded polymer-rich nanoclusters and aligned crystallites that increase tensile toughness and modulus at least twofold compared with fibers produced without antisolvent control or without post-drawing. Related Work: Existing approaches to produce high-performance bioinspired fibers fall into several classes: (1) highly aligned crystalline synthetic fibers (e.g., UHMWPE) that deliver high strength/modulus but low extensibility and high creep; (2) artificial-silk strategies that mimic β-sheet crystallites via molecular design, crystallization, or mineral/organic reinforcement to raise stiffness but often sacrifice ductility or scalability; (3) hydrogel- and supramolecular-fiber methods that exploit noncovalent interactions and phase separation to add extensibility, moisture responsiveness, or self-healing but typically deliver limited strength/toughness; and (4) covalent or hybrid crosslinking schemes that improve toughness but reduce reversible, humidity-responsive behavior. Major limitations across these methods are inability to simultaneously achieve textile-grade strength, high toughness, large elastic recovery, high damping, and humidity-actuated supercontraction in a scalable wet-spinning process; limited process control over microphase morphology during coagulation/wet-spinning; and sparse demonstrations of combining controlled microphase separation with post-drawing strain programming at scale. Abstract: We address the challenge of producing scalable hydrogel-based fibers that simultaneously achieve high toughness, textile-grade strength, reversible elastic recovery, high damping, and humidity-actuated supercontraction. We propose a wet-spinning pipeline that leverages antisolvent-induced microphase separation in ultrahigh-molecular-weight sodium polyacrylate (PANa)–polyacrylamide (PAM) composite hydrogel dopes and post-spinning uniaxial strain programming under controlled humidity. The process maps antisolvent polarity, hydrogel pH, and PAM/PANa composition to form hydrogen-bonded polymer-rich nanoclusters, and uses post-drawing to align polymer chains and induce oriented crystallites. The main contribution is a validated fabrication-to-structure pipeline that produces fibers with hierarchical aligned microfibrils, dense hydrogen-bonded nanoclusters, and β-sheet-like composite crystallinity, delivering combined properties (target toughness ≈100–120 MJ m−3, strength ≈150–200 MPa, high damping, and >50% actuation) in meter-scale fibers. Expected outcomes include a reproducible parameter set for scalable wet-spinning of multifunctional hydrogel fibers and quantitative structure–property correlations linking microphase features and strain programming to mechanical and actuation performance. Experiments: Samples and variables: prepare PANa–PAM hydrogel spinning dopes at fixed PANa concentration (0.073 g mL−1) with PAM/PANa mass ratios f ∈ {1/6, 1/4, 1/2, 1}. Adjust dope pH ∈ {4.1, 4.6, 7.0, 9.2}. Coagulate into antisolvent baths: IPA, EtOH, MeOH, and MeOH/water (7:3 mass ratio). Post-drawing: apply uniaxial prestrains ∈ {0%, 100%, 200%, 300%, 400%} at 75% RH, then stabilize at 65% RH for 6 h. Replicates: n = 5 independent fibers per condition. Baselines: (A) fibers spun into IPA without methanol (minimal microphase separation), (B) fibers produced without post-drawing, (C) commercial UHMWPE fibers, and (D) representative reported hydrogel fiber. Characterization: morphology—SEM, TEM, AFM (topography, modulus, adhesion); nanostructure—SAXS (1D, 2D) and WAXS for orientation/crystallinity; chemistry—FTIR (hydrogen-bonding signatures); water uptake—gravimetric RH series (35%, 55%, 65%, 85% RH). Mechanical testing: uniaxial tensile tests at 65% RH, strain rate 2 mm min−1, measure fracture stress, fracture strain, Young’s modulus, and toughness (integral of stress–strain). Dynamic tests: cyclic loading 20–100% strain to quantify dissipated energy and damping (%) over 5 cycles and 100 cycles. Actuation tests: thermal (40–120°C) and humidity (85% RH) supercontraction: measure actuation strain, actuation stress, work per mass (J kg−1). Energy absorption: free-fall impact damping using fixed mass drops, record acceleration/time to rest. Microstructure–property mapping: compute orientation factor from WAXS azimuthal FWHM; quantify SAXS scattering intensity and correlation length of nanoclusters; quantify AFM modulus contrast. Ablation studies: (1) hold f=1/4,pH=4.1 and vary antisolvent polarity to isolate microphase separation effect; (2) hold optimal antisolvent and f and vary pH to test protonation role; (3) vary prestrain while keeping all other parameters constant to quantify strain-programming contribution. Evaluation metrics and acceptance criteria: at least 2× toughness improvement over baseline A and baseline B; orientation factor increase monotonic with prestrain; correlation coefficient R>0.8 between SAXS intensity (cluster density) and toughness across conditions. Statistical reporting: report mean ± standard deviation, perform ANOVA across primary variables and post-hoc pairwise tests for n=5. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: uncontrolled antisolvent diffusion during coagulation can produce nonuniform microphase morphologies and variable fiber diameters; insufficient hydrogen-bond network formation may prevent formation of discrete nanoclusters or oriented crystallites; post-drawing under humidity may cause slippage or necking leading to fracture before target alignment. Data/evaluation biases: mechanical results are humidity- and temperature-sensitive; small-sample laboratory measurements (n=5) may overestimate reproducibility for large-scale production. Scalability and process constraints: large-scale wet-spinning requires solvent handling and recovery for methanol-rich baths and precise humidity control during post-drawing; solvent residues may affect biocompatibility. Materials limits: approach may be limited to hydrogen-bonding-compatible polymer pairs and may not generalize to systems lacking carboxylate/amide chemistry. Long-term stability: reversible hydrogen-bond networks may exhibit creep or property drift under sustained load, repeated cycling, or variable environmental exposure. Characterization limitations: SAXS/WAXS and AFM provide local information that may not capture mesoscale heterogeneity along meter-scale fibers. Safety and environmental constraints: use of methanol and large solvent volumes introduces toxicity and flammability hazards that constrain industrial translation.
